text: Twisted and folded back on itself, and so hard to follow from one end to the other — the word of choice for a tax form, a legal contract or a plot with too many characters. It began as a word for literal folds, which is why the wrinkled surface of a brain is described as convoluted. Dr Hegemann applies it to the chain of molecular steps inside a human eye: light strikes one protein, which alters a second, which alters a third, and only at the end does an electrical signal appear.

To subsist is to stay alive on whatever you can get, keeping going on the bare minimum rather than thriving. A subsistence farmer grows food to eat rather than to sell, and soldiers cut off from supplies subsist on rations. Here it names how the alga makes its living: it eats nothing at all, surviving entirely by turning sunlight into chemical energy.

Someone awarded a major honour, most often a Nobel prize. The word remembers the ancient custom of crowning victors and poets with a wreath of laurel leaves, so a laureate was once literally the person wearing the laurels. It survives in a few fixed titles you will meet again, including Nobel laureate and a country's poet laureate. The Nobel in each science can be shared by at most three people, which is why this article has exactly three.

Literally a large metal disc struck to make a booming note, but in British usage a gong is also slang for a medal or an official award — the kind pinned on you at a ceremony. The subtitle says the inventors of optogenetics get the gong, a deliberately offhand way of saying they won the Nobel prize. The joke is the mismatch between the grandest prize in science and the most casual possible word for it.

Strange, unconventional, coming from a direction nobody expected — an off-the-wall idea, an off-the-wall sense of humour. The image is a ball bouncing off a wall at an angle you cannot predict. Calling the study of a pond alga's eyespot the most off-the-wall scientific research is the article's way of saying it looked useless and turned out to be anything but.

In British English, to work something out is to figure it out — to reach an answer by reasoning or calculation, nothing to do with exercise. Here it states the point of optogenetics: switch one kind of brain cell on and you can work out exactly what that cell does. The same sense turns up in everyday phrases like I can't work out why he said that.

This phrase does two unrelated jobs within a few lines of each other, so read it carefully. To turn something out is to manufacture it in quantity: the frogs' eggs turned out the desired proteins. But to turn out to be something just means to prove to be it in the end, which is what those proteins did when they turned out to be light-stimulated ion channels.

To come to someone's rescue is to arrive with exactly the help they needed at the moment they were stuck. It works for a person who pulls you out of trouble and, as here, for a thing: Dr Hegemann could not test his guess with the tools available, and the new science of genomics came to his rescue. The phrase always implies the help was both timely and decisive.

t: Great oaks from little acorns grow
forms: Great oaks from little acorns grow
text: An English proverb: enormous things grow from tiny beginnings, so do not dismiss something merely because it starts small. An acorn is the seed of an oak, a nut you can hold between two fingers, and an oak is among the largest trees in Europe. The article closes on it as a joke about scale — a whole scientific field grew out of one single-celled pond alga, so the writer amends the proverb to little algae.

A French expression taken whole into English, literally reason of being, meaning the single purpose for which a thing exists. You reach for it when one function is the entire point of something: the raison d’être of a fire extinguisher is to put out fires. Describing neurons as cells whose raison d’être is the transmission of electrical signals means carrying signals is not one job among many but what they are for.

To compress is to squeeze something into a smaller space, and by extension to pack a process into fewer steps or less time. Hegemann's hypothesis was that the long chain of molecular events found in a human eye had been compressed in his alga — the same end result reached in one step instead of several. It does not mean the alga was physically squashed; what shrank was the number of stages.

Besides meaning to demonstrate that something is true, prove carries an older sense: to turn out to be. Testing his guess proved hard means the testing was hard, not that anything was demonstrated. Watch for it in front of adjectives — the journey proved longer than expected, the rumour proved false — where it is simply a more formal way of saying turned out.

Beyond the thing you use to find a street, a map is any systematic chart of how the parts of something are laid out. A map of the DNA of Chlamydomonas is a record of the order of its genetic material with the positions of individual genes marked; biologists talk about mapping a genome. The point in the article is that once such a map existed, Hegemann could look up candidate genes instead of hunting blindly.

To enlist is to sign up for military service, but to enlist someone is to recruit them to help with your project. Dr Hegemann enlisted the assistance of a colleague — he went and asked him in, and got him working on the problem. The word suggests actively persuading somebody to join rather than simply receiving help that was offered.

Harvesting is gathering a crop, but in biology and medicine it means collecting cells, tissue or organs from a living source for use somewhere else. Kidney cells harvested from hamsters and from human embryos were taken from those sources and then kept alive in the laboratory. It is the standard term in this field and carries no suggestion of farming.

In biology, to culture cells is to grow them deliberately outside the body, in a dish of nutrient liquid held at the right temperature. So cultured rat neurons are live nerve cells from a rat, growing in laboratory glassware rather than in a brain — nothing to do with being refined or well-read. The distinction matters here, because a result in cultured cells is much weaker evidence than the same result in a living animal.

In science, a paper is a published report of one piece of research, written to a strict format and printed in a specialist journal after other scientists have checked it. Saying the paper announcing this finding was published in 2005 fixes the date the result went on the public record, which is what normally settles who was first. Counting the field's thousands of papers is a rough way of measuring how much work has been done.

Observe can mean to watch closely, but it also simply means to remark or to point out. An audience member at the announcement observed that Dr Miesenböck might be miffed — they said it out loud. The two senses sit close together, since a remark of this kind is usually a comment on something the speaker has noticed.

The everyday sense is the thing you deal with first. In science, priority is a technical term with a sharper meaning: the credit for having been first to make a discovery, usually settled by the date a result was published. Regardless of details of priority means setting that argument aside — which matters here, because Miesenböck published related work three years earlier and did not share the prize.

Beyond blowing up, to explode is to grow suddenly and enormously: demand exploded, the population exploded. Saying the subject has since exploded means the number of researchers and published papers on optogenetics shot up very fast after 2005. The image behind it is something expanding too quickly to be contained.

No deception involved here. In science and engineering a trick is a clever technique that gets around an awkward problem, usually one somebody had to invent. The trick of threading extremely thin optical fibres into a brain to illuminate groups of neurons was a real piece of ingenuity, and calling these tricks is praise. You will meet the same approving sense in a neat mathematical trick.

To conceive of something is to form the idea of it in your mind, to think it up; the same root gives conception, an idea at the moment it is born. Deisseroth conceived of putting channelrhodopsin-2 into neurons — nobody had proposed it before, and the proposing is what he is credited for. Keep the sense of originating an idea separate from merely understanding one.

Literally what a plant does when it comes into flower, used figuratively for anything developing quickly and promisingly. The blossoming science of genomics was a young field growing fast in the 1990s, not yet mature. It is a warm word, which is why you would never describe a growing problem as blossoming.

An appendage is a part that projects from a main body — an arm, a leg, a tail, an antenna. Biologists reach for it as the neutral umbrella term when they do not want to commit to calling something a limb. The thin appendages here are the alga's two flagella, the whip-like threads it swims with.

To hypothesise is to put forward a hypothesis: a specific proposed explanation that you can then go and test. It is stronger than guessing and weaker than concluding, and that middle position is exactly its value in science — Hegemann hypothesised that the long chain of steps was compressed in his alga, then went looking for evidence. The spelling with an s is British; American writing uses hypothesize.

Mildly annoyed, put out, a little offended — a deliberately low-key word, nowhere near furious. Saying Dr Miesenböck might have serious reason to be miffed is British understatement: he did comparable work earlier and was left out of a Nobel prize, so he has grounds for rather more than mild irritation. The gap between the size of the grievance and the smallness of the word is the joke.

A single-celled green alga, shaped like a pear and found in ponds and damp soil worldwide, which swims using two whip-like flagella. It is one of biology's workhorse laboratory organisms: cheap to grow, simple, and with its DNA sequenced early. The two-part Latin name follows the standard convention — Chlamydomonas is the genus, reinhardtii the particular species.

Alga is the singular of algae: a simple photosynthetic organism that lives in water and has no true roots, stems or leaves. The group runs all the way from single cells like Chlamydomonas to seaweeds metres long. Note the irregular plural, which trips people up — one alga, many algae.

Flagella are slender, whip-like threads projecting from a cell, which lash back and forth to drive it through liquid. Chlamydomonas has two of them and uses them to swim towards light; a sperm cell moves the same way. The singular is flagellum, from the Latin for a small whip.

An eyespot is a patch of light-sensitive pigment and protein on a simple organism — not an eye, because it forms no image and has no lens. What it can do is register which direction light is coming from, which is all the alga needs in order to steer towards it. The reddish eyespot of Chlamydomonas is where this whole Nobel-winning story began.

A photosynthetic organism lives by photosynthesis: using the energy in sunlight to build sugars out of carbon dioxide and water. Plants, many algae and some bacteria do it, and it is the reason there is oxygen in the air. Calling Chlamydomonas photosynthetic explains why it bothers to swim towards light — light is its food supply.

The laboratory technique this prize honours: putting the gene for a light-sensitive protein into chosen cells, so that shining light on them switches those cells on. The name is built from opto, meaning light, and genetics, since the light-sensitivity is delivered as a gene. Its value to neuroscience is precision — you can activate one type of neuron at an exact instant and see what the animal does.

The set of annual international awards established by the will of Alfred Nobel, the Swedish chemist who invented dynamite, and first given in 1901. There are prizes in physics, chemistry, physiology or medicine, literature, peace and economics; the science prizes are announced each October and can be shared by at most three people. They are generally treated as the highest honour in their fields, which is why being left out of one is worth remarking on.

The study of the nervous system — brain, spinal cord and nerves — covering everything from the chemistry of a single cell up to memory and behaviour. It is a modern umbrella field that draws on biology, chemistry, psychology, physics and computing. A neuroscientist is anyone working in it, and the article's claim is that optogenetics changed what they are able to find out.

The retina is the thin sheet of light-sensitive tissue lining the inside of the back of the eye, where light is turned into electrical signals for the brain. It is the human structure this article sets against the alga's eyespot, and the comparison is unflattering: the retina's chain of molecular steps is some twenty times slower. Damage to it causes blindness even when the rest of the eye is sound.

A protein shaped roughly like a tube that sits in the membrane around a cell, with a passage through the middle just wide enough for particular charged atoms to cross. Because the membrane otherwise blocks charged atoms, opening these channels lets them move and shifts the voltage across the membrane — and that voltage swing is the electrical signal a nerve cell carries. Channelrhodopsin-2 is an ion channel whose pore opens when light falls on it.

The branch of biology that reads and studies whole genomes — an organism's complete set of DNA — rather than one gene at a time. It became practical in the 1990s as sequencing machines grew faster and cheaper, which is why the article calls it blossoming at that date. It rescued Hegemann's project by handing him the alga's full DNA sequence to search.

The particular protein at the centre of this story: an ion channel from Chlamydomonas whose pore opens when blue light strikes it, letting charged atoms cross the cell membrane. Its name joins channel to rhodopsin, the family of light-absorbing proteins that also includes the ones in your own retina. Put its gene into a neuron and that neuron can be switched on with a flash of light.

Drosophila melanogaster, the small fly that gathers around ripe fruit, and one of the most heavily used animals in all of biology. It breeds in about ten days, costs almost nothing to keep in a bottle, and its genetics have been picked over for more than a century. Miesenböck's earlier work used a light-sensitive protein from a fruit fly rather than from an alga.

An optical fibre is a hair-thin strand of glass or plastic that carries light along its length, bouncing it off the inside walls so it follows bends without escaping. The same technology carries internet traffic under the oceans. Deisseroth's contribution was to thread extremely thin ones into a living mouse brain, so that light could be delivered to a small group of neurons deep inside.

A group of inherited eye diseases in which the light-sensitive cells of the retina gradually break down, usually narrowing vision from the edges inwards over years and often ending in blindness. There is no cure, which is why it attracts experimental approaches. The attempt mentioned here is to use optogenetics to make surviving cells in the retina light-sensitive again, giving the eye another way to respond to light.
